items.title: Capturing Time: Review of the Zero Image Pinhole Camera by Taylor Blanchard
items.content:
This post may contain affiliate links. If you click on a link and make a purchase, Shoot It With Film may receive a small commission at no additional cost to you.

Written by Taylor Blanchard

I have a few cameras that feel like an extension of me: cameras that produce images that most reflect who I am and help me creatively express my ideas. My Zero Image Pinhole is one of those cameras.

It’s not necessarily easy to use, but at its heart, it’s the embodiment of film photography – light passing through a small aperture and recording an image on film. No batteries, no lenses, no image framing window.

Find the Zero Image Pinhole Camera at the Zero Image website.

As the pandemic was ramping up in early 2020, Blue Moon Camera sent an email that they were receiving a shipment of cameras from Zero Image, a Hong Kong-based camera company that makes wooden cameras in a variety of formats.

Zero Image was shutting down for the foreseeable future given stay-at-home restrictions. In the U.S., we were a few weeks away from that fate. I’m not sure what resonated with me most: the beautiful wood camera? The thought of purchasing a camera from a company that couldn’t make cameras for a while? Or a typical case of GAS (gear acquisition syndrome)? 

Whatever the reason, I clicked “add to cart” – buying one of the medium format (120 film) models. A few months later, well into stay-at-home orders in the U.S., the camera arrived. It was as beautiful as I had imagined, and quite intimidating. While it’s a simple rectangle box camera, it doesn’t look or feel easy to shoot in the way a plastic camera or a point and shoot does. 

Zero Image was launched in 1999 by Zernike Au, a “pinhole enthusiast” who had a successful career as a product designer, according to the company’s website. When Zero Image launched, its website says there wasn’t another roll film pinhole camera company in existence. The cameras are constructed of teak wood and brass and finished with a wax or varnish, depending on the model. Several retailers carry the brand, but the cameras are often out of stock.

Unboxing and Setting Up the Zero Image Pinhole Camera

There are several models of Zero Image; I bought the 69D Deluxe “Back to Nature” edition. I think it’s named “Deluxe” because it comes with added features: a bubble level, a 52mm filter thread, and a cable release adapter (the naming of these cameras is a bit confusing to me). All the 69 models can shoot 6×4.5, 6×6, 6×7, and 6×9. Back to nature refers to the wood finish: a wood oil versus a varnish.  

Zero Image pinhole cameras arrive in a subtle cardboard box. The camera comes with a basic instruction manual that provides a basic overview of loading film, exposing film, and caring for the camera.

As I mentioned, the camera design is simple. On the front of the camera is the filter thread, a brass cable release adapter, and the shutter. The pinhole size is 0.17mm and the focal length is 40mm for an equivalent aperture opening of f/235.

The top of the camera has two brass knobs – one to lock the top wood plate in place; the other is a film advance winder. The bubble level is also on top of the camera. The back of the camera has a sliding cover with 3 red windows to reveal the film count: the upper window is for 6×4.5, the middle is for 6×6, and the bottom is for 6×7 and 6×9. There is also a brass dial on the back which acts as an exposure scale to guide your exposure calculations. 

To adjust the film format size and load the film, remove the top cover and then slide out the back cover. Two dividers allow you to adjust the aspect ratio. I generally shoot the same aspect ratio with this camera, although you could adjust it every time you load film.

The film loads on the left side of the camera; the film moves from left to right. Loading the camera can be a bit tricky, even once you’re accustomed to the process. You drop the film into the right side slot and then roll the 120 paper leader onto the take-up spool, ensuring the spool snugly fits behind a metal guide. You then slide the back cover on and fasten the top onto the camera. You must line up the slot on the take up spool with the film advance knob. Finally, tighten the center knob.

Then, turn the film advance knob clockwise to move the film. You move the film until the number 1 appears in the window that matches the format that you set. The red window is similar to several other cameras with red windows, like a Holga or Brownie.

Related: An Overview of Pinhole Film Photography: Exposure, Reciprocity, & 6 Cameras I Love

Moving from ‘Meh’ to ‘Marvelous’

The first year or so I owned this camera, I enjoyed it, but I didn’t connect with the camera. I thought the exposures didn’t render the results that I expected. Following the exposure dial on the back of the camera and using a light meter app, I felt like all my shots were way under- or over-exposed, and I didn’t like the images I was getting. I muddled along with the camera, never loving it.

Then, two things changed. First, I adjusted the aspect ratio from 6×6 to 6×9. I’m not sure why I defaulted to shooting 6×6 when I first got the camera, as I already have several cameras that shoot that format. I find it easier to frame my photos and pre-visualize the scene with 6×9, since it’s almost as wide as the camera. The 6×9 format also creates more expansive images (and, yes, I eventually want a camera that shoots 6×12).

Next, my friend Alec Pain helped me with the exposure calculations. To get more accurate exposures, I follow the multi-step process that he later published for Shoot It With Film. The two biggest changes I made were calculating the exposure specifically for f/235 and then accounting for the reciprocity characteristics of the film. Before I had been winging it with exposure, which can sometimes lead to good results, but never consistent results.

I started to play more with the camera and push the limits of shooting with it. Instead of always reaching for a film with a good reciprocity quality, I would look in my reciprocity app for the films that need multiple minutes of light for a minute of measured exposure. I frequently use filters, typically a red or IR filter, which add even more exposure time, for creating self-portraits or photographing the environment around me. The results of these long exposures feel like capturing time as a continuum and not a fixed instant.

With these changes, the camera is the one I turn to for many ideas and projects. I love carrying it when I travel, even though it takes more effort to use. It’s one way to capture a frequently photographed scene in a new way.

One of My Favorite Cameras, Broken

As I was pondering the outline for this article, the worst happened: the camera started to wobble on the tripod, so I unscrewed the tripod plate to investigate – accidentally pulling off the tripod thread and the wood that was holding it in place. That point of the camera is often under pressure with the tripod, plus I am often taking the tripod plate off to move to another camera, which might add additional tension. I emailed Blue Moon Camera to see if they had any ideas, and someone named Jed (I think) called me back.

He’d had the same thing happen to his Zero Image camera and we chatted through some ideas on how to fix it. I ended up screwing the plate back into the camera, slightly offset from the previous screw holes into wood that is still stable. Next, I need to get a product like Liquid Nails to secure it further.

It’s something to keep in mind with this, or any wood camera. I always keep mine stored in a Domke wrap, in a plastic bin with some silica gel packets. But, I also tote it around with me, and it’s definitely been dinged up and exposed to the elements.

I thought the tripod base would have been sturdier and, honestly, am a bit surprised that the wood would have become that soft. I also found it reassuring that it happened to someone else, although it begs the question how many other people have experienced this issue?

Conclusion

While anyone can make a pinhole camera with household materials (and it’s a fun activity for kids and adults), generally you don’t have as much control. With a Zero Image (or similar brand) pinhole, you know the exact aperture opening and can calculate your exposures. It’s an amazing camera to test the limits of a film stock and push yourself creatively.

The wood is gorgeous and eye-catching and often prompts conversations with passersby. I would hope that subsequent versions of the camera have a stronger base for the filter thread. I’ll continue to use the camera for as long as possible, even if I have to keep gluing it!

What do you think of these wood pinhole cameras? Let me know what you think in the comments!

Thank you so much, Taylor! Taylor is a regular contributor here at Shoot It With Film, and you can check out her other articles here, such as Phoenix vs. Ektachrome: Is Harman’s Color Film a Slide Film Alternative? and Shooting Film on a Budget: Color Films Under $10.

You can also check out more of Taylor’s work on Instagram.

Today, we’re featuring a wonderful Florida Keys photo story from film photographer Caitlin Cisar. Scroll below to view the images and read more from Caitlin about exploring the Keys…

Film in the Florida Keys

By Caitlin Cisar

Flying with film means I always play the fun-time-at-airport-security-game where I ask them to handcheck my bag of film. Honestly, it’s a bit of a hassle for everyone so I get it; but this trip I tried something different. I pre-purchased my development and brought a bubble mailer with me so I could drop it in the post-office before catching my flight back home.

I headed to the Florida Keys with a roll of Kodak Gold 200, LomoChrome Turquoise 100-400, and my trusty Minolta X-7A + Minolta 50mm F/2 lens. Part of why I love shooting film is because I love the simplicity and tactile experience of this camera and lens. I zoom with my feet, manually set the exposure with my in-viewfinder meter, and hold my breath when the shutter speed is low.

I also love to try experimental stocks, which is why I included a roll of Turquoise in my bag. I started in Key Largo (the top island of the Keys) and chose ISO 400. I am always pleasantly surprised with color shift film; while I know things will be different, exactly which other worldly effects are a fun surprise. Jurassic Park vibes were not on my radar, but I love the result!

Kodak Gold is my everyday film stock otherwise, and I figured it would be especially nice for some leisurely travel photos in a tropical setting. There’s something already warm about both the color and contrast combination, and it can really work for a range of situations. I loaded this next and headed south.

The Florida Keys have a rich history. A must-do for history buffs is a stop at Pigeon Key, which is accessible by walking, bicycle, or tram across the old Seven Mile Bridge. Renting bikes made the 4-mile trek a breeze (literally) which was a nice reprieve from the heat.

Upon arriving at Pigeon Key, there is a small fee to explore the island. You get access to bathrooms, a gift store, a museum, and if you time it right, you can see the shark feeding.

The story goes that the pool used to be for humans—those who worked on the bridges and railways. Eventually it was taken over, and the new owner removed a corner to accommodate boat parking. Sometime later, with the current ownership, the pool is now home to sharks and fish exclusively. Every month the gates are opened and the sharks can swim out, however, they always return, likely because it is a safe home for them. Edgar (the bird) also lives on the island full-time.

Heading further south to the bottom of the Keys is Key West, which has the famous (and busy) Duval Street filled with restaurants, bars, roosters, and beautiful architecture. A stroll that is worth a few shots on Gold around sunset.

After finishing the film rolls, I dropped the mailer off at a post office and hopped on my flight care-free. A week later, the photos were in my inbox. This was nice not only to avoid traveling back with the film and then deal with packing it up, but it also motivated me to truly “shoot it with film.” Having a deadline and mission made me excited to spend time taking photos as one of my travel activities. I’ll definitely be doing this method again and am excited to try out different stocks in new locations!

items.title: Photographing Concerts and Live Events on Film by Angela Izzo
items.content:
This post may contain affiliate links. If you click on a link and make a purchase, Shoot It With Film may receive a small commission at no additional cost to you.

Written by Angela Izzo

Photographing a live event feels as though I’ve been transported back to the very place where my love for photography first took root—somewhere between the music, the people, and the electricity of live shows.

As someone who has always chased experiences, I found myself completely immersed in the world of music from as early as I can remember. I spent years traveling with bands, losing myself in venues, moving effortlessly between backstage, onstage, and the heart of the crowd. Every moment carried its own kind of magic, and every experience became part of the way I learned to see.

Long before I realized it, those nights were shaping not only my perspective but also the eye I would eventually bring to photography. Looking back now, it all feels like living inside the film Almost Famous—a life measured by songs, stories, and the beautiful chaos that exists between them.

An Unexpected Film Camera for Live Events and Concerts

Looking back through these concert images—some taken more than a decade ago—I’m reminded of what I love most about photography: its ability to preserve a moment that can never be recreated. These photographs are more than documentation of a performance; they’re fragments of a feeling, a time, and a place.

While I was always drawn to the energy onstage, I found myself equally captivated by the people in the crowd—the friends, the strangers, and the quiet moments unfolding between songs.

Although I often carried professional digital cameras, I almost always had my tiny Diana Mini with a flash tucked away. That little camera captured a kind of magic the larger equipment never could.

Small enough to slip into any venue, it invited curiosity instead of intimidation. People would light up when they saw it, letting their guard down in a way they rarely did in front of a larger camera. Those unguarded moments became some of my favorite photographs.

As a professional photographer, I often carried large camera bodies and lenses—gear that required credentials and full press access to get where I needed to be. But when I wanted to move through the night more casually and capture moments without drawing attention, I always reached for a small film camera. I’d choose just one to carry, keeping things light for the long haul.

The Diana Mini quickly became a favorite. With up to 72 frames on a single roll, it allowed me to document an entire night in a fluid, spontaneous way. It wasn’t about technical perfection—it was about preserving the energy, the movement, and the moments.

The Benefits of a Small Camera

Many of the shows I photograph are ones where I’m invited by the band or already know the artists, which gives me the opportunity to arrive early and spend time backstage. Those moments become my favorite photographs.

In those settings, a small film camera is an advantage. In my experience, it’s far less intimidating to security, venue staff, and the people around me than a full professional digital setup.

The moment you walk in with large cameras and lenses, you’re more likely to be stopped, questioned, or asked for credentials. But with a compact film camera, I can move through the space more naturally. I can blend into the crowd, experience the show as a guest, and capture authentic moments as they unfold.

Related: Diana Mini Camera Review

Choosing a Film Stock That Matches the Event

One of the most important considerations when shooting film is choosing the right ISO for the environment.

If I’m photographing outdoors during the day, I can usually shoot without a flash using a film stock rated between ISO 100 and 400. But when the light starts to fade—or I’m shooting indoors at a concert or event—I reach for ISO 400 to 800 film and switch on my flash. That combination gives me the flexibility to embrace the atmosphere while still capturing the energy and spontaneity of the moment.

Choosing a film stock comes down to the look and feeling you want to create. For my documentary-style approach, I like to keep things simple with a 35mm color film at ISO 400. It’s versatile enough to handle most concert environments while staying true to the moment.

If you’re looking to experiment, though, film offers endless creative possibilities. You can play with different color palettes, specialty film stocks, or embrace more abstract, unpredictable results. I’ve even photographed shows with a Polaroid camera. It’s certainly bulkier to carry than a compact film camera, but awesome for that instant gratification. Makes it well worth the extra space in my bag.

Getting Close to the Action

Photographing artists onstage with a film camera can be more challenging than shooting digitally. Depending on the lens you’re using, your images may lean toward a softer focus, or you may not be close enough to capture the moment the way you envision it. That’s part of the unpredictability—and the charm—of shooting film.

When I’m photographing in a smaller venue, though, everything changes. Being able to stand onstage or just a few feet from the artists makes it much easier to create intimate, dynamic images. That proximity allows me to capture not only the performance itself but also the connection between the musicians and the audience in a way that feels immediate and personal.

Capturing the Atmosphere

One of my favorite parts of photographing live shows is capturing the atmosphere beyond the stage. I’m drawn to the people just as much as the performers—their style, their energy, and the way they express themselves, especially when a show has a theme. The audience is part of the story, and I love documenting the personalities that make each event unique.

Whenever I see someone whose look catches my eye, I’ll stop and ask, “Can I take your photo?” More often than not, they’re excited to say yes. I think there’s something disarming about holding a small film camera or a Polaroid. It feels less like paparazzi and more like an invitation to create something together.

Those nostalgic cameras encourage people to let their guard down, making it easier to capture an honest portrait that reflects who they are in that moment.

Using Creative Techniques

When I’m photographing events, I love experimenting with techniques that push beyond documenting the moment. Double exposures and prisms are some of my favorite creative tools, adding a surreal, dreamlike quality that echoes the energy of live music.

Whether I’m shooting Polaroids or 35mm film, I always embrace the pop of an on-camera flash. It gives the images a raw, documentary feel. With cameras like my Diana, I can layer exposures and create soft, overlapping frames that exaggerate motion and atmosphere.

Sometimes, I’ll pair those techniques with an experimental film stock, introducing bold colors or  textures that add another layer of personality to the photograph. 

Final Thoughts

My biggest piece of advice is to stay present and truly observe your surroundings. It’s easy to get caught up in the chaos of a show, but sometimes the best photographs come when you step away from it.

If the crowd feels overwhelming, move to a different corner of the venue or look for a new perspective. Changing your point of view can completely transform the story you’re telling. Every concert or live event has countless stories unfolding at once—the magic lies in discovering the one that speaks to you.

Whenever I have a camera in my hands, a sense of calm settles over me. It’s almost meditative. My camera becomes an extension of myself—my brush, my eye, and at times, my shield.

Through the viewfinder, I become completely immersed in the world around me, searching for the details that others might overlook: the light or a gesture, the movement of the crowd, or a quiet moment between the noise. Those are the pieces that come together to tell a story.

items.content:
This post may contain affiliate links. If you click on a link and make a purchase, Shoot It With Film may receive a small commission at no additional cost to you.

Today, we’re featuring a lovely photo series from film photographer Ausra Linkeviciute. Here is more from Ausra about photographing Highgate Cemetery…

Highgate cemetery in North London has long been a place I loved to visit and photograph. And yet, having photographed it before with my digital cameras, something was always missing – the depth and richness of that green color, the peacefulness, stillness, and mystery of the place… This time I ventured out with my new Mamiya, still with the excitement of just learning to use it. At one moment, I came across an incredible scene tucked away in the corner above all the crypts. There was a white carpet of petals under the tree with a doorframe in the background, and in the light breeze, more petals were still falling. I spent a long while at this spot, and instead of snapping away on my DSLR (had I brought it), I took just two images. This time, I knew this was finally the right camera, as looking at the final image I felt all the same emotions I did when standing there. That to me is the power of film I am in the process of discovering – this ability to bring back a physical trace and the emotion of the place we are capturing.

items.title: A Keyring Camera That’s Not Digital. Try the Baby Holga! by Alec Pain
items.content:
This post may contain affiliate links. If you click on a link and make a purchase, Shoot It With Film may receive a small commission at no additional cost to you.

Written by Alec Pain (Alastair Place)

I recently purchased a digital keychain/keyring made by Holga (find on eBay). It’s similar to the Kodak Charmera, only it’s been beautifully designed to replicate their old “Baby” Holga, the Holga Micro 110.

It got me thinking about how nice it would be to re-make it – and provide analog film photographers with a keychain/keyring that isn’t digital! I’ve asked Holga and … there’s a possibility… but I think I’ll need a large number of you to buy one!

Find the Holga Digital Keychain on eBay here and the Baby Holga/Holga Micro 110 on eBay here.

110 Film Photography

There are two fantastic articles written by my fellow Shoot it with film writers about 110 film photography. The first is by Angela Izzo: 110 Film: What Is It & Everything You Need to Know.

The second is by Katya Rowny: Pentax Auto 110 Review: A Nostalgic and Unique Pocket Film Camera.

Where to Buy a Baby Holga

If you do a search for the Baby Holga or Holga Micro 110 on eBay, you’ll find that it came in a number of different colors. I have the Yellow, Red, and actually Black. The latter formed part of an Oyakö set of a Baby Holga and a Mummy/Daddy Holga 120FN and distributed by superheadz.

The others are very tricky to get hold of, with Red the most available. Ebay has a couple – and the cost has started to rise for such a little camera!

My advice? The Japanese website buyee.jp – an excellent website for locating old and out of production Holgas, Dianas, and plastic cameras! They “buy” the camera for you and take care of the postage for a small fee and you can also buy several things and have everything posted at once.

How to Use the Baby Holga

In the meantime, I’ve started taking pictures with the Holga Micro again. Essentially, it’s a very, very simple camera. It means you need to think carefully about what you are going to take and be mindful of the camera’s lack of control.

The camera (according to instructions if you are lucky enough to find one with the camera when buying secondhand) has a focal length of 25mm, an F8 aperture and a shutter speed of 1/125 second. The focus is 1m to infinity. Pretty much standard Holga in terms of the aperture and shutter speed.

To load the camera, you pull down the back cover (it can be a little tight) and pop your 110 film cartridge in. Close the back cover, and then wind the film advance wheel (located at the front of the camera on the right when the “lens” is facing you) until it reaches the first number. It should stop there. If it doesn’t, take the cartridge back out and make sure it is inserted properly.

The Viewfinder is folded neatly on the top of your camera so needs to be pulled up with your thumb or finger, in order to compose your shot. Hold the camera around 4-5 cms away from your eye when looking through it, and depress the tiny shutter release button on the back (right) of the camera. Then, wind onto the next shot.

Bear in mind that the camera is either on the end of your keyring or in your pocket, so if you are going to put it away, the button can often be pressed accidentally. If you have finished shooting for the time being, it’s best to not forward the film to the next number as you might end up with the odd blank shot.

Film Available for 110 Cameras

Lomography is the only company right now producing 110 film. There are various expired films available, but for the purposes of this article I’ve not shot Orca (I have a roll being developed!) or Classicolour. I couldn’t tell the difference with the Color ‘92s when I came to scanning them:

Lomography B&W Orca 110 ISO 100
Lomography LomoChrome Classicolor 110 ISO 200
Lomography Lobster Redscale 110 ISO 200
Lomography Color Tiger 110 ISO 200
Lomography LomoChrome Turquoise 110 ISO 100–400
Lomography LomoChrome 2021 Metropolis 110 ISO 100–400
Lomography LomoChrome Color ’92 ISO 400
Lomography LomoChrome Color 92 Sun Kissed ISO 400
Lomography LomoChrome Purple 110 ISO 400

There are a couple of triple packs available, too, but the savings are minimal.

Taking the Baby Holga Out

Previously, I had shot it during Holga Week on a trip to Norwich and Cromer. I was most impressed with the portraits I took of my friend the photographer @jayhaldon:

You can see some light leaking onto the bottom of the film but not the actual image. This being a Holga, you’ll find that the light leaks can sometimes edge onto the image area. I think shooting into the sun doesn’t help.

I love the way that the image ghosts itself in various degrees onto the surroundings, and I think I prefer seeing the Lomochrome writing on top of the image.

More casual “street” shots at Norwich station also came out well and benefitted from the 400 ISO film.

More recently, I’ve been testing several of the cameras I have. Here’s a shot pointing into the sun (barely shielded by a light cloud), but it still produces a pleasing image, and I was able to find some detail in the shadows with LomoChrome Tiger ISO200.

Related: The Holga 135 Pan: Getting to Know Your Camera

LomoChrome Turquoise

LomoChrome Turquoise seemed to produce the best images – perhaps because I was pointing the camera at London landmarks.

As you can see from the image on the second image below, it does take some getting used to when looking through the viewfinder with the Palace of Westminster trying to get in on the scene!

I took some portraits of my wife with the camera, and you can see the sun behind her creeping into the picture:

And flowers always look good on Turquoise:

Scanning (and Developing) Your Tiny Negatives

I did find scanning the negatives problematic. The images are tiny and my scanner (an Epson V700 photo) went from producing beautiful images like those below to very grainy pictures which I couldn’t improve.

There is a 110 film holder available here, but you could also use Lomography’s digitaliza. I’m waiting for mine, but I scanned the negatives on my flatbed scanner – with two pieces of glass holding them. I managed to get a reasonable resolution on them, but not always!

You can also develop the negatives yourself. I bought two little reels from @Film Stuff Lab in the US which was very reasonable if you live in the States, and I hope to start developing soon! I also found these 110 reels on Amazon.

The smaller your negative, the larger your hairs and icks, so get used to using the healing tool in Photoshop!

Looking at the two here side-by-side of Big Ben, I’m still not sure which I prefer.

LomoChrome Metropolis

LomoChrome Metropolis also seemed suited to the brighter sunshine. The Lomo 92 seemed to struggle in really bright light (unlike the Mummy/Daddy Holgas).

LomoChrome Tiger

Tiger was also lovely in bright sunlight – note the light leaks:

And here’s a missing frame when placing the Holga in my pocket, traveling from (19) Oxford Street window to next day (21) the South Bank:

You can also get some inconsistencies when scanning:

And I did seem to get a few scratches on my Yellow Holga – along with some moiré when scanning too:

Lomo 92

A trip to Scotland gave me the chance to try out some landscapes, and these, too, were a little inconsistent when scanning:

In cloudy conditions in Weston-Super-Mare, Lomo 92 produced muddy and duller imagery.

Lomo Redscale “Lobster”

I did love this Redscale study of a High Rise in Lewisham:

The Baby Holga Project

It’s safe to say that I have renewed my love for the Baby Holga, so much so that I have started a little project: The Baby Holga Project (@thebabyholga). I already owned two of the Baby Holgas, an orange and a black one, and have since purchased quite a few more.

I have started sending them around the world. Currently, there are four travelling around the US. Three are in the UK, three in Europe, one in Hong Kong, one in Argentina, one in Canada, one in Africa and two in Australia/New Zealand.

Check out the Instagram page to see what’s happening or who has which Holga. If you would like to participate, please DM @thedailyholga or @thebabyholga.

items.title: Point & Shoot Camera Roundup: 3 Film Cameras Worth Checking Out by Katya Rowny
items.content:
This post may contain affiliate links. If you click on a link and make a purchase, Shoot It With Film may receive a small commission at no additional cost to you.

Written by Katya Rowny

Over the past few years, we have had an influx of new film cameras arrive on the scene (talk about an oxymoron!). From the half-frame Pentax 17, to the Rollei 35AF from MiNT, and most recently the Snapic A1 from Kodak.

Unfortunately, most of these cameras are not cheap, with the range being in the $100’s for the Snapic and the $500s for the Pentax 17. I have to admit, I am not impervious to all of these new models and makes, and have been secretly coveting the Snapic A1 for a while.

In an attempt to further dissuade myself from acquiring more cameras, (did you read my other article where I mentioned I have a slight camera hoarding problem?) I decided to re-examine my collection of point and shoots and remember why I fell in love with them in the first place.

1. Chinon Bellami

First up is the Chinon Bellami (find on eBay). Also known as the Revue 35CC in some markets. This camera is one of those surprisingly cool cameras that often flies under the radar. I picked this camera up at a swap meet for under $20 and was drawn in by the size and unique design.

Introduced in 1980 as a competitor to the Olympus XA series, it packs a lot into an incredibly compact body. Instead of a traditional lens cap, the Bellami uses a clever “barn door” mechanism that opens when you advance the film, revealing a sharp 35mm f/2.8 lens Chinonex Color lens.

The Bellami uses automatic exposure, has a fast shutter ranging from 1/8 to 1/1000 second, and simple zone focusing. This camera slips easily into a pocket, has a quiet shutter, and requires very little thought beyond estimating your focus distance. The perfect grab and go camera.

In everyday use, the Bellami proves to be more than just a cute little camera. The camera handles exposure automatically, leaving you free to focus on composing your shot, while simple zone-focus settings keep operation straightforward. I was impressed by the image quality of my prints, noting that the lens produces sharp photos with rich colors and strong contrast despite the camera’s age.

Combined with a satisfying film advance, quiet shutter, and lightweight design, the Bellami is fun and effortless to shoot. While it may not be as well known as some of its contemporaries, It has become one of my main go-to’s when I want to quickly capture memories instead of focus on settings.

Read the full Chinon Bellami review here.

Find the Chinon Bellami on eBay.

2. Olympus XA2

The Olympus XA2 has earned a reputation as one of the best compact film cameras ever made, and it’s easy to see why. I can’t rave about this camera enough; I recommend it to anyone who will listen. Small enough to slip into a pocket, simple enough for beginners, and capable of producing fantastic images, it’s the kind of camera you can take anywhere.

Released in 1980 as a more user-friendly version of the original XA, the XA2 swapped the rangefinder for a simple zone-focus system while keeping the iconic sliding clamshell cover. Paired with the sharp 35mm f/3.5 Zuiko lens and automatic exposure, it offers a great balance between convenience and image quality.

What really makes the XA2 special is how easy it is to shoot and the image quality. Open the lens cover, set the focus zone for your subject, and let the camera do the rest.

This camera is the perfect travel companion and everyday carry camera, thanks to its lightweight design, quiet shutter, and consistently sharp results.

Like any camera that’s over 40 years old, it has a few quirks—aging electronics that may need some extra attention and occasional light leaks can happen—but those drawbacks are minor compared to everything it does well.

I have captured some of my favorite images on this camera, and it has traveled to many countries with me. For anyone looking for a reliable, pocket-sized film camera that delivers great photos without a lot of fuss, the XA2 remains one of the best options out there.

Read the full Olympus XA2 review here.

Find the Olympus XA2 at KEH Camera or on eBay.

Related: 12 Best Point and Shoot Film Cameras

3. Olympus Trip AF

Last but not least, the Olympus Trip AF (find on eBay) is one of those cameras that you may pass over but deserves a second glance, especially if you’re a fan of the legendary Olympus Trip 35.

Introduced in 1984, the Trip AF represented Olympus’s move into the new wave of electronic point-and-shoot cameras. Unlike its metal-bodied predecessor, the Trip AF is mostly plastic and built around convenience. It features a 35mm f/3.5 Zuiko lens, manual film advance and rewind, a built-in flash, and a surprisingly simple autofocus system with just two focus points—roughly 1.5 meters and 4 meters.

Exposure is fully automatic, with shutter speeds ranging from 1/85 to 1/250 second and apertures from f/3.5 to f/11, making it a true grab-and-go camera. You can check out the manual here.

The Trip AF line was part of Olympus’s broader AF (Infinity in the U.S.) family of autofocus compact cameras. Compared with the Trip AF, premium models like the AF-1 offered a faster 35mm f/2.8 lens, closer focusing, a wider range of shutter speeds, DX coding, and accessories like teleconverters and close-up lenses.

The AF-1 Twin expanded the idea with both 35mm and 70mm lenses, while later cameras like the AF-10 XB featured a wide 29mm lens and a large, bright viewfinder. The biggest difference between the Trip and AF models was that Trip cameras focused on maximum simplicity with fixed shutter speeds, while AF models offered more advanced, program-controlled exposure systems.

Find the Olympus Trip AF on eBay.

Final Thoughts

Some of these cameras are more well-known than others, but every one of them has earned its place as a great compact point-and-shoot. Whether you’re just getting started with film or you’ve been shooting for years, you really can’t go wrong with any of them. The right choice simply comes down to how much control you want over your photos.

As tempting as it is to chase the latest hyped-up film camera, I often have to remind myself that I already own some amazing cameras that are more than capable of producing beautiful images. The truth is, there are plenty of affordable and often overlooked cameras out there—you just have to know what features matter most to you and do a little hunting.

The only question that remains is which one will you choose?

Thank you so much, Katya! Katya is a regular contributor for Shoot It With Film, and you can check out her other articles here, such as 12 Months, 12 Cameras: The Film Photography Project That Changed How I Shoot and 5 Unconventional Ways to Find Your Inner Artist.

You can also find more of Katya’s work on her website, Instagram, and YouTube.

Japan Travel Story

By Autumn Kovach

Kyoto, Japan was the third and final city on my Asia itinerary after Vietnam and South Korea in October, 2025. It was a very anticipated destination based on countless peoples’ reviews and reverence for the country. I was curious if I would come away feeling the same as I had heard it described.

I enjoyed the clean streets, cute cars, and multiple temples. I tried not to have too much of an American experience and seek out truly local spots, but it was fun to see Blue Bottle Coffee; a familiar place from living in New York and visiting San Francisco in the US.

I aim to avoid capturing people’s clear identity when I travel. For me, it just feels too vulturistic, and with the fact that it is illegal to photograph people without their consent in Japan, it provided me with an additional container to photograph blurred motion in order to capture the energy of the people there and at a respectful distance.

When I arrived I found a film store right away and saw a LomoChrome Color ’92 film that I spontaneously decided to play with. Even within the first couple of hours of arriving, Kyoto felt immediately nostalgic, like I was in an old movie and for the first time I believe I captured a place on film in exactly the way I was experiencing it. I loved how this film highlighted the muted colors, the subtle textures and clean lines of the city. I truly felt like I was on the outside looking into a place or even looking back in time with such curiosity and awe.

items.title: The Last Two Frames: Finding a 70-Year-Old Roll of Film in a Vintage Camera by Artem Feofilov
items.content:
This post may contain affiliate links. If you click on a link and make a purchase, Shoot It With Film may receive a small commission at no additional cost to you.

Written by Artem Feofilov

I love Paris in the spring time
I love Paris in the fall

Frank Sinatra

Despite the epigraph, we have mixed feelings towards Paris. We came here in August 2011 because I’ve got a contract with Sorbonne, and the first acquaintance was a disaster – renting an apartment, bureaucracy, problems with language, nothing resembled our impressions of visiting this city as tourists.

But, the time passed by, we found an apartment, got our residence permits, learned the language and understood what to visit and what to avoid. Then, I got a permanent position, we settled down to the South of Paris, and started enjoying living in France.

This is just one thread that leads to the story I want to tell.

A Love of Analog

The second thread is linked to our inclination to “old school/analog” perception of the world.

Don’t get me wrong, I started reading e-books back in 1996 when I’ve got my first personal computer. I have gigabytes of digital music on my hard drives, and I’ve been working with data processing for a quarter of the century. But, we found that listening to vinyl music adds something to the experience – you enjoy opening the envelope, reading the lyrics and watching the 30cm photos, you clean the dust, lower the needle and you do not skip the tracks.

The same is for analog photos – it’s needless to tell in this community that taking analog pictures is different from working with digital cameras. You do not take the camera out of the bag unless you see that the picture is really worth it. You compose carefully and push the button.

Later on, you develop the film without knowing for sure that the result will satisfy you – lots of things can go wrong, from stubborn film not wanting to get into spiral to problems with chemistry. Then, you hang the film to dry it and see that technically it looks OK, but you don’t know whether it is what you wanted.

Finally, you scan and edit it and get 6 keepers out of 12 shots if you are lucky. But, this way you remember all the shots you’ve done.

Exploring Paris Flea Markets

The third thread is linked to our two hobbies – biking and visiting flea markets. We live in 22km from the heart of the city, and, sometimes, we just jump on our e-bikes and make a tour. If we are lucky, we pass by a flea market and stop by.

Flea markets in France are very different, offering from next-to-trash to next-to-museum selection of items. Sometimes, you may find a real gem like a set of carved wooden chairs dated by the beginning of the previous century in decent state for less than 100EUR.

With respect to our “analogue hobbies,” the flea markets offer a limited selection of vinyl disks (repeating themselves almost everywhere, with few exceptions) and sometimes old photo cameras.

Finding a Time Capsule

This time we’ve hit two birds with one stone.

First, we noticed a couple of unknown vinyls and got them from the sellers: a talkative slightly drunken mustached man in his fifties and a young couple sitting in the van. Then, I noticed an unusual camera sitting in a brown leather case on their table.

Both the camera and the case were in unusually good shape given the apparent age – no fungus, no mold, no rust. The mechanism seemed to work, too.

But, the selling point for me was that I saw that the film counter showed “2” in the small window. For those of you who are not familiar with the medium format cameras of that era, I need to say that the numbers are printed on the back of the paper separator of the film itself, so if you see the number, the film is inside.

The sellers were surprised to learn that that their camera contained a potential time capsule, but they didn’t bother and didn’t change their intention to sell it. So, for the price of a lunch for two in a cheap place, we’ve got the camera.

Related: What Makes a Good Film Camera Part II: Why Craftsmanship Matters

Developing the Images

When we came home, I extracted the film from the camera – it was Kodak Verichrome Pan 620.

Since the sensitivity was not indicated, and the conditions of shooting/storage were not known, I decided to use a stand developing process. In this case, you dilute a tiny amount of a developer in water, just right to let the chemistry do the job slowly and be dumped after. The stand developing process takes about one hour and requires little to no agitation. It works well for the scenes when you need to have detailed shadows without burning whites. It also works well for the unknown films.

The only problem was that the nearly 70 year old film was extremely stiff and kept the memory of all these years sitting tightly rolled. It just didn’t want to get into spiral even after being soaked in lukewarm water for a couple of hours. Finally, I just put a paper towel between the layers of film to let the developer do its job.

When I pulled the developed film out of the developing tank, we saw the images with a naked eye, without any need of scanning and editing the curves.

Decoding the Images

When I did the scans, we realized that this is a real time machine. Let’s try to decrypt the images and assign them to the time period, event and place.

The time frame is defined by the following parameters: the “Drépy” camera was manufactured from 1945 to 1953; it was the “French response to the Germans,” an in-house design based on German so-called “clap cameras” of the Voigtlander type.

Those days, the price of the camera was the equivalent of one month and a half salary of a qualified worked, and one can feel this – it’s solid built, the material quality is high and the bellows are light-tight after all these years.

I checked the speed accuracy – it’s on the slow side, but one should have expected this. Based on the lens clarity and the mechanics I’d say that the camera will shoot gain.

The film is Kodak Verichrome Pan 620; its production began in 1956 and didn’t end until 1995.

Next, there are cars in the square; the Citroën 2CV is clearly identifiable with a license plate that appears to be on a light background—this is from before 1963. The corrugated hood on the Citroën is from before 1960. Overall, this was an iconic car, very typical for France in the 50s and 60s.

The men in suits also suggest the 1950s rather than the 1960s, when the dress code became relaxed. The boy in shorts and sandals with socks is also from the 1950s. The woman in a knee-length skirt indicates that we’re in the second half of the 1950s. Before, the skirts were below the knee and in the 1960s, they were above the knee. There might be also a 1-3 year offset between the capital and the province, but most probably we’re still in the 1950s with this skirt.

If we put all these dates together, we get somewhere around 1957–1959.

Now, what kind of event is this? Clearly a religious one, but which one? Judging by the colors in the courtyard photo, it’s spring or summer. A communal celebration — First Communion — is typically held around the time of Catholic Easter.

The belt/garment resembles a monastic order like the Franciscans, but to go further, we’d need to consult experts to determine in which schools or regions of France religious traditions were still strong during those years. France is not really a very religious country; there are plenty of churches, but you don’t see many parishioners.

As for the location — based on a vegetation and sunshine, I’d say that it’s northern or central France, and these are the regions with a strong Catholic tradition back in the 1950s.

So, here we have this completely unexpected trip down memory lane. We can only guess why a good camera with undeveloped film was put on a shelf, or why the boy in the photo didn’t inherit it and start using it. I could have suggested a few storylines, but they will be highly speculative. You may suggest your own in the comments.

Gear used:
Rolleiflex 1950 + EpsonPerfection5870 or PentaxK20D in macro-mode for scanning

Love Letter to the Sonoran Desert

By Alicia Schmidt

Hi, my name is Alicia. I am just a girl who loves light, film, and her small piece of the Sonoran Desert.

This is my love letter to the Sonoran Desert. I’m not from Phoenix originally, although a good portion of my adult life has unfolded here—begrudgingly. I didn’t choose this place. It chose me.

I’m here to tell its story through my eyes—
in light-wrapped desert plants,
in streaks of light sweeping across the landscape,
in wide, open skies with stems reaching, that hold both the past and what has yet to come.

I’m here to witness the seasons as they shift, and the way nature moves with them—
the quiet, serene winter,
the wild, untamed spring,
the harsh, burning summers of this place.

The desert is resilient, but also relentless—in a way I had never experienced before.

In the Sonoran Desert, I lost myself. I didn’t trust my voice. I feared the worst—and many times, I lived it. I’ve cursed the heat, the harshness, the sun beating down on my skin. I’ve questioned why I was even here at all.

My journey with photography didn’t begin here—but my journey with film did.

Film requires surrender. It requires trust.

For a long time, I relied on external validation for my worth. I put my camera down for years. I was afraid—of failure, maybe even of success. I compared myself. I shrank myself. I told myself my art wasn’t good enough.

Still, the desert called. The light called.

Eventually, I picked up my Pentax K1000 again and made a quiet commitment—to show up.

And in that decision, something shifted.

I began to see my eye form.
The way I’ve always seen the world—
light wrapping around stems,
glowing through leaves,
revealing softness where others might only see harshness.

It was never about clients, or being accepted, or being celebrated.
It was about expression without expectation.

This journey became about seeing—
light, shadow, environment—through my own eyes.
What brings me into presence.
What makes me breathe deeper.
What stirs awe.

And in that, I found my way back—to photography, to the Sonoran Desert. And most importantly – to myself.

What began as an initiation by fire has become my love letter.

This place adopted me. Took me in as its own, showed me extraordinary in the ordinary.

It changed me.

I love you, Sonora.

Alicia Dominique

items.title: What Makes a Good Film Camera Part II: Why Craftsmanship Matters by Tyler Mattas
items.content:
This post may contain affiliate links. If you click on a link and make a purchase, Shoot It With Film may receive a small commission at no additional cost to you.

Written by Tyler Mattas

This is going to essentially be an unintended part two of my previous article – so if you didn’t read it or don’t remember it, maybe start this article by reading that one.

On said article, a certain Adam S. posted a comment that resonated with me and inspired this addendum. Adam noted that much of what I was describing as contributing to a good camera boiled down to engagement with a well-crafted piece of engineering – something that transcends cameras. I couldn’t agree more, and it’s an idea I’d like to explore further here.

More Than the Final Image

As I sit here writing this, like a dozen rolls of film are also sitting nearby on my kitchen table, still undeveloped after being shot on vacation a month and half ago. I’ll get them developed eventually, but in the meantime it doesn’t bother me all that much that I still don’t have my photos. In fact, I’ll probably end up shooting even more rolls to add to the pile before I finally mix up chemicals.

What I’ve realized while thinking through this “good camera” stuff is that what really drives me to shoot film is what Adam pointed out far more succinctly than I did in my prior article.

I actually primarily enjoy using the cameras that I shoot with – even more so than I actually enjoy seeing the resulting images.

Yes, I know plenty of people do film photography for the film photos (shocking, truly). I’m not knocking anyone’s reason for shooting film, especially since shooting photos for the photo’s sake is probably the most logical and obvious reason. For me though, the act of using and engaging with the tool actually turns out to be of primary importance.

I know I’ll probably be crucified for this assertion, including by fellow Shoot It With Film writers (Katya, looking at you), but this is exactly why I’ve never found cameras like the Holga, Ektar H35, all late ‘90s and on Tupperware SLRs, hell even the new plastic fantastic Rollei 35AF, appealing.

Maybe it’s even part of why I don’t like shooting with Sony digital. It has nothing to do with image quality or usability. It’s not gear snobbery. The cameras are just too appliance like, too utilitarian, too ugly – putting it shortly, too… modern.

As I lamented in the prior article, everything we interact with these days looks, feels, and often performs like it was designed and manufactured with a bare minimum “that’ll do” mindset. Everything keeps getting more expensive while simultaneously getting worse. Never mind transcending just cameras, this seems to transcend products generally and has bled into architecture, art, entertainment, etc., but alas that’s a whole other article.

The Lost Art of Craftsmanship

There was a time not long ago when skilled people took great pride in their work. Businesses took pride in their products. Product longevity, fit and finish, innovation, and even beauty were top priorities – and it showed in the tools produced.

Tools that myself and certainly others, (judging by Adam’s comment) seek out and enjoy engaging with to have a user experience that simply doesn’t exist (or is increasingly hard to find) in modern versions.

You’ll never see something like a Contax IIA created again. Pentax showed us not that long ago that people hoping even for a new production K1000 were engaging in wildly wishful thinking (delusional thinking might be more bluntly accurate).

Even Leica who still has the price capacity to do interesting things, just keeps trending more and more in this Apple-like direction of $8,000 minimalist black boxes that look like a 3 year old’s conception of a camera.

With few exceptions (those exceptions being obvious, just look at who has the mile long waiting lists, over MSRP scalpers, never in stock, etc.), cameras over the past several decades have gone the same way as all the other products: uglier, crappier build quality, more uniform and uninteresting, etc. And maybe that’s really the appeal of vintage products generally. They tend to be… not those things.

Manufacturers actually recognize this, too, because there’s been a trend across industries to make vintage looking products.

This actually works when the products also live up to the vintage build quality (Olympus enters the chat) or when the consumer base doesn’t care about the build quality (Dodge enters and quickly exits the chat).

It fails miserably when the manufacturer doesn’t understand that the looks are only part of the magic and cannot single handedly carry a cheap feeling, plastic-y ambassador of the cost cutting department (Nikon sadly avoids the chat)… unless you’re Dodge.

Related: What is a Rangefinder? And is It the Right Film Camera for You?

The Vintage Appeal

Not coincidentally, people into film cameras tend to be into other vintage products as well. I found a lot of the same appeal and enjoyment in mechanical watches that I’ve found in vintage film cameras, and for all the same reasons.

It still blows my mind that I’ve simply disassembled, cleaned, and lubed century old watches… and I have a working watch that keeps good time. Try that with your A7IV in the year 2120.

It amazes me that in 1890 someone didn’t just do the already extremely intricate work of building a watch, by hand, but then also took the time to elaborately hand decorate parts of the movement that would then be covered with a case and never seen again until the watch was serviced a decade or more later.

Today that would be called a waste of time and fall victim to the first round of cost cuts. Does it tell time? Good enough. Ship it.

Make a camera with all brass internals? Madness. Some injection molded plastic will do just fine for the 90 day warranty period. Serviceability? We just need it to last those 90 days so we don’t have to give them another one; when it breaks on day 91 they can throw it out and buy a new one.

Elaborate decorative ironwork on a street light? You must be crazy. Someone just go install a raw metal pole with a bulb on it, puts out the same light.

I find this mentality and everything it produces, and I mean everything, annoying and disheartening. Actively getting away from it by seeking out interactions with products and tools (mostly vintage) not made with this mentality helps me maintain my sanity.

Final Thoughts

So alas, whether it’s film cameras, vinyl records, vintage clothes, classic cars, mechanical watches, or whatever old stuff anyone might be into – I think a lot of us are here for the same reason.

We’re all reaching back to an age when the products we interacted with didn’t just get the job done or get it done in the most utilitarian way possible.

They made us admire their craftsmanship, they made us want to look at them because they were beautiful, they made us… want to use them. That’s what makes a good camera – or good anything else.

Thank you so much, Tyler! Tyler is a regular contributor here at Shoot It With Film, and be sure to check out his other articles, like What Makes a Good Film Camera? It’s Not as Simple as It Seems and Repairing Your Own Film Camera: Lessons I’ve Learned.

items.content:
This post may contain affiliate links. If you click on a link and make a purchase, Shoot It With Film may receive a small commission at no additional cost to you.

Written by Angela Izzo

“You can learn a lot of things from the flowers…”

That line from Alice in Wonderland stayed with me from a young age. I remember watching Alice stumble into a patch of flowers and they suddenly come to life. That’s how flowers have always felt to me: as if they exist in a world of their own, each with a distinct personality waiting to be discovered if you look closely enough. 

There’s a fleeting moment when a flower reaches its peak before it begins to fade away. Through photography, I’m able to capture that brief moment of beauty and preserve it, allowing it to stay with me forever.

My Favorite Ways to Photograph Flowers

For me, flowers serve as an inspiring backdrop when I create photoshoots. I love the splashes of color and the natural textures they bring to an image—it never gets old to me.

I often place my model among the flowers and layer the images through double exposure using different film stocks like 120, 35mm, 110, or even newer Polaroids with double-exposure capabilities. Even without layering, flowers create a beautiful texture that adds a magical quality to the image.

Through my work, I want the viewer to feel transcended to another time, drawn into a fantasy, or even overwhelmed by the richness of textures and layers that flowers can create.

As most of you know, I love mixing and matching different cameras and film stocks, especially when photographing flowers as my muse.

If I want to create something more surreal, I’ll reach for films like Psych Blues or Lomography Lomochrome, which have a way of transporting you into another world through their unexpected tones and colors.

Each camera has its own unique quality, and I use them as part of my ongoing exploration of the many ways a flower can be captured — whether it’s serving as the backdrop, the main subject, or even a prop within the frame.

There’s really no wrong choice when it comes to the camera itself. What I’m most drawn to are the layers, textures, and colors that different combinations bring to an image, and the way they can transform something familiar into something dreamlike and new.

A Few Tips for Better Film Images of Flowers

1. Slow Down and Really Study the Flower

One thing that helped me improve my flower photography was taking the time to really look at the flower before taking the image.

I pay attention to how the light hits the petals, the way it glows, the shape, and even how the wind moves it. Sometimes just waiting a few extra moments can completely change the feeling of the photograph.

2. Mix Different Cameras and Film Stocks

I love experimenting with different cameras and film because each combination creates a different mood. Some film stocks make flowers feel dreamy and surreal, while others bring out softer natural tones.

Playing around with different looks really helped me find my own style and made the process feel more creative and personal.

3. Learn Your Camera Through Trial and Error

A lot of flower photography comes from experimenting and making mistakes. I used to get too close trying to achieve that macro look without understanding my lens, and my images would come out blurry or out of focus.

Over time, learning my camera’s strengths, depth of field, and how to work with distance helped me create images that felt more intentional and true to my vision.

Related: Floral Macro Photography on a Budget – No Macro Lens Needed!

Common Mistakes when Photographing Flowers

One of the most common mistakes people make when photographing flowers is either using the wrong lens or getting too close to their subject. If you don’t fully understand your camera’s depth of field and focusing range, moving in too close can leave most of the image out of focus.

I think many photographers are drawn to that detailed macro look, but without the right lens or settings, the flower can end up looking more like a blurry blob than a sharp, intentional image.

That’s also part of the beauty of photography — trial and error. Learning your equipment is essential to achieving the results you’re looking for.

Another important thing to pay attention to is light. Too much sunlight combined with a high ISO can easily blow out your image and wash away the delicate details of the flower.

You have to slow down, study the light, pay attention to the wind, and consider your distance from the subject. When all of those elements come together, they help create a successful image.

Final Thoughts

The next time you’re out on a walk or driving through town, take a moment to notice which flowers are blooming and how they change with the seasons. Pay attention to the trees and plants around you, how long their blossoms last, and the quiet beauty they bring to everyday spaces.

If you happen to have a camera with you, slow down and really study them — the way the light moves through their petals, the shape of their form, and the small details that often go unnoticed. Sometimes the simplest subjects can become the most inspiring when you take the time to really see them.

Flowers have a way of reminding us to appreciate fleeting moments and the beauty that exists all around us. Maybe that inspiration will lead you to create an image that feels meaningful and uniquely your own. Most of all, remember to slow down and stop to smell the roses.

items.title: No Tripod? No Problem. Double Exposures with Neon, LED Screens, & Contact Sheets by Alec Pain
items.content:
This post may contain affiliate links. If you click on a link and make a purchase, Shoot It With Film may receive a small commission at no additional cost to you.

Written by Alec Pain (Alastair Place)

I’ve been working on sets of images using neon and LED screens for a couple of years now.

Being out late at night (often having an hour or so to kill before my train departs to take me home) and without a tripod, I wanted to experiment with Neon signs and then rewind the film and shoot over the top of them with fresh images, creating double exposures.

Experimenting with Neons & Double Exposures

I had been wandering around Oxford’s Westgate shopping centre – with all of the shops closed and only the odd person heading up the escalators to the second-floor restaurants and only had some expired Ferrania Solaris film left to play with. I hadn’t thought much beyond the neon signs and, so, once I had finished the roll, I simply rewound the film and though perhaps I would just shoot more neons.

There are plenty of options for you to double expose – if your camera can double expose straight away then that’s a bonus. If not, you will have to rewind the film and shoot the same roll again.

The Minolta CLE has a manual winder so it is relatively easy to reload the film. Hold the camera up to your ears until you hear the click of the film being released from its holder and the leader will be sat there waiting for you.

I’ve done similar double exposures with an old Nikon and this does require that you have either a film retriever or a spare piece of film to get the leader back.

For the second set of shots, I walked around and happened upon an LED screen in the Flannels window playing adverts for various items of clothing. As it was dark, the bright lights of the LED screen gave enough light to get sufficient exposure and bring out the neons I had shot earlier.

I love the way that it worked out. Seemingly random neon signs – like the “fussy suckers” one here below lined up perfectly with the Gucci kids looking mardy.

There were other moments of synchronicity. This chap’s red jacket and the green of the Backstreet Becky’s (and the Pho sign too), also seemed to match perfectly.

Film Edges & Making the Images into Art

My lab – The Mini Lab – provide me with superb scans – and they’ll scan the film in longer strips so that I can join the film up into one long piece – but they don’t, as yet, scan the sprocket/edges of the film.

This means I often do some scanning of my own once I get the negatives back. This is easiest with a larger scanner, but you can do this with a DSLR and a stand.

I own an Epson v550 scanner which has now stopped scanning negatives. Getting a consistent exposure on the whole roll (and lining up of everything is a slow and laborious process but one that I think is worth your while). The scans aren’t quite as vivid as the ones you get from a lab, but I believe that the whole reel scanned in (a little like a contact sheet) makes roll itself a work of art – a beautiful larger format image for my wall.

This is done by stitching everything together in Photoshop (or other image editors). I usually line everything up as one long strip, before cutting it down into a contact sheet. (See my article here).

Scanning the end of the film and the start of it also adds some variety. It turned out that Ferrania Solaris also had some beautiful red circles and + signs on the sprockets and really fit in well with the red feeling of some of the images.

I then cropped it down to form a 4×6 image which was more easily printable than a longer format. I love the way the people interact with the neons and the film edges:

Related: Scanning Film Borders with the Epson V600

Vertical Contact Sheet

I tried the same technique using portrait images.

This time I used the screens at London’s famous Piccadilly Circus as my first set of exposures. I then rewound the film and used the LED screen at the British Film Institute (BFi) on London’s South Bank.

This is Candido 800 and the film didn’t have the visual interest on the edges of the film that Ferrania did, but again I got some lovely color and cross over images with it.

It’s a lot grittier than the “Fussy suckers” roll – but I love the final piece of jagged pixelisations and eerie imagery from the films that were on show at the BFi.

Using the Holga 120N for Sprockets.

Scanning film with sprockets can be even more time consuming. I shot the sprockets using the Holga 120N. You can learn how to do that here.

I found it difficult to line up the sprockets – especially when scanning with my DSLR and then color correcting. The labs scans were so much more vivid – and it’s always really interesting to see what your own edit brings to the piece.

Mine aren’t anywhere near the quality which a lab can bring to your scans, but unless you can get your lab to scan them, you make a trade off with colors and some sharpness.

It’s up to you what the final finished piece looks like and finding detail and bringing it out of the negative to me is more important than “well that’s how the scanner scanned it in”!

These exposures are both from a walk down Oxford Street (and possibly Marylebone), some nine to twelve months apart. The problem with the Holga is that you need a dark bag to rewind the film (unless you intentially double expose whilst you are shooting), so I had to wait till the next time I was in London late at night to take the second lot of images! I have a portable dark bag now which I’ll take along with me in order to rewind the film in future.

I’ll continue working on these and try and get my scans less blue (and I’m looking at a new scanner) but when seen as a whole I love the complete set. You can see the difference in scans from the lab as opposed to mine below:

Again, picking out some of the bits that work together produce several works of art as well as the overall one.

I particularly loved the juxtaposition of the young boy and the Unleaded Diesel petrol station neons.

Failure Sometimes Leads to Success

Sometimes a whole roll has failed me totally, and, yet, I’ve still created an artwork from the ruins!

This one was an attempt at using the very wide Holga 120PAN with 35mm film – in an attempt at getting the sprockets filled with color.

I don’t think it was actually at night! The back of the Holga wasn’t sufficiently taped up leaving a square block where the light leaked through. I turned it into a full roll of abstract art:

In Conclusion

I hope you love this technique of shooting double exposures at night and creating digital contact sheets. I can’t wait to try this out further.

I still got some nice photos on the RB67, but that was more useful during slower, scenic experiences. items.title: Rediscovering Street Photography: Slowing Down and Experiencing the Moment by Raufan Yusup
items.content:
This post may contain affiliate links. If you click on a link and make a purchase, Shoot It With Film may receive a small commission at no additional cost to you.

Written by Raufan Yusup

I honestly can’t remember the last time I did street photography. A year ago? Maybe even longer?

What I do remember is how my focus slowly shifted, toward water, swaying trees, or as simple as a little corner I found during my walks. At some point, I simply stopped enjoying street photography the way I used to. It happened without me even noticing.

That shift deepened when I started shooting with larger formats, first 6×6 medium format, then 4×5 large format film. I began to slow down, soaking in the scene before committing to that one precious (read: expensive, lol) shot.

But recently, I was back on the streets! A friend and I went to the Sanja Festival in Tokyo and to be honest, I enjoyed both the session and the results, but in a different way.

Getting Back Out There

The Sanja Festival (Sanja Matsuri) is one of Tokyo’s most vibrant and energetic traditional festivals, held every May in Asakusa. It celebrates the three founders of Sensō-ji Temple, enshrined at the nearby Asakusa Shrine.

For three days, the streets come alive with hundreds of mikoshi (portable shrines), traditional music, and a sea of energy from the crowds. It’s a wild, joyful mix of spirituality, community pride, and street-level intensity, a rare and beautiful glimpse into Tokyo’s cultural soul.

For this outing I brought two cameras: the Nikon FE loaded with Ilford XP2 400, and the Minolta TC-1 (find on eBay) with JCH Streetpan 400.

The TC-1 was an easy choice. It’s tiny, almost invisible in a crowd, and that 28mm Rokkor lens is just remarkable for something that fits in your palm. The FE on the other hand is more deliberate. Manual focus, manual exposure, it actually nudges you toward being selective rather than reactive. I used a 50mm lens as well for the FE which is a little bit tricky for this kind of situation. But that felt right for the headspace I was in. I wasn’t there to shoot fast or shoot a lot.

Next time though, I’m genuinely curious what it would feel like to bring my Fuji GW690ii. Medium format at a festival sounds kind of wild, probably impractical, but maybe that’s exactly the point. The added ritual and weight of it might push me even further into that observational, unhurried mode.

Learning to Slow Down

After I got the film back from the lab, I found myself reflecting: Why did this feel different from before? Why did I unexpectedly enjoy it? What changed?

One of the things I realized is that, in the past, I was always chasing faces. That’s what street photography meant to me: getting close, capturing expressions. But it came with a constant sense of hesitation and discomfort. To be honest, I often felt like a thief, stealing someone’s face without permission.

But after spending so much time slowing down, shooting landscapes, little corners, and using slower formats, I think I’ve started to see things differently. This time, I didn’t approach street photography with the same urgency or pressure. I wasn’t looking to capture people’s faces. I was simply enjoying the moment, letting the festival unfold around me, and photographing it with care.

What pulled me in were the moments, the things happening all around me. The mikoshi being carried through packed streets, surrounded by people in happi coats, the whole procession moving like one living organism.

There’s something about Sanja Matsuri specifically that makes this so compelling. It’s not just a street scene, it’s one of the most iconic festivals in Japan, and you can feel that history and collective pride in every direction you point your camera.

Related: Street Photography: The Importance of Practice

Experiencing the Moment

One frame I keep coming back to is from the TC-1, a shot of the procession where the crowd and the shrine and all that energy happen to line up together.

I wasn’t trying to isolate anyone or wait for a decisive moment in the classic street photography sense. I just raised the camera when the scene felt whole. There was no pressure in it. And I think that’s exactly why it worked.

Another one from the FM2 is a wider view of the shrine with the crowd spreading in every direction, layers of people and signage and movement all in the same frame.

In the past I would have tried to cut through all of that and isolate something specific. This time, I let the chaos be the subject. That feels like the most honest way to show what Sanja Matsuri actually feels like to be in.

It felt more like documenting an experience than intruding on it. I wasn’t trying to “get the shot,” I was just there, present, observing, enjoying. And I think that shift is what made this time feel so different.

Final Thoughts

Maybe that’s something worth remembering: when we stop enjoying something, sometimes all we need is a little distance, a chance to step back, see it from a new angle, and come back to it in a different way.

Will I return to shooting street photography more often? I’m not sure. Maybe I will, but probably not as frequently as before. Right now, I’ve found comfort in small corners of the streets, flowing water, and the soft light of sunset. That’s my safe space for now.
